title: The diffusion of large language models in published academic articles.
corpus: Full texts of 7.3 million journal articles from four publishers (Elsevier, Frontiers, MDPI, PLoS); 228 focal words
headline_estimate: An estimated 57% of published articles in 2025 (12% in 2023) showed evidence of LLM influence
verbatim_quote: By 2025, an estimated 57% of published articles exhibited evidence of LLM influence, up from 12% in 2023.
notes: PNAS 2026 (PMID 42213755, doi 10.1073/pnas.2605754123). Abstract cited via PubMed; Europe PMC record not yet indexed. Authors: "Among articles exhibiting LLM-influenced text, there is substantial heterogeneity, ranging from subtle linguistic influence to articles mostly or entirely LLM-generated", so the figure is share of articles with LLM-associated language, not share of LLM-written text.

title: Have Large Language Models Enhanced the Way Civil & Environmental Engineers Write? A Quantitative Analysis of Scholarly Communication over 25 Years
corpus: 149,452 abstracts published by the American Society of Civil Engineers (journals and proceedings), civil and environmental engineering
headline_estimate: 13.9% (2024) and 20.4% (2025) of abstracts likely LLM-written (conservative); frequency-shift estimate 15.3% and 26.2%
verbatim_quote: A more conservative multi-marker classification procedure, based on a global marker word set derived from these years, yields corresponding estimates of 13.9% and 20.4% of abstracts likely written by LLMs.
notes: Quote from full-text passage. Same passage: the frequency-shift method gives 15.3% in 2024 and 26.2% in 2025; thresholds give a pre-2023 false-positive rate of ~1% and a 2024-2025 classification rate of ~17%. Domain range in 2025: 15.6% (geotechnical) to 38.4% (construction).

title: How much are LLMs changing the language of academic papers after ChatGPT? A multi-database and full text analysis
corpus: Abstracts in six databases (Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, PMC, Dimensions, OpenAlex); 2.4 million PMC open-access full texts
headline_estimate: Frequency of "delve" up 1,500%, "underscore" up 1,000%, "intricate" up 700% between 2022 and 2024; not a share of papers
verbatim_quote: Across databases, delve (+1,500%), underscore (+1,000%), and intricate (+700%) had the largest increases between 2022 and 2024.
notes: Reports term-frequency growth, not the share of papers written with LLMs. Also: in PMC full texts the proportion of papers using "underscore" six or more times rose by over 10,000% from 2022 to 2025.

title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary.
corpus: More than 15 million PubMed biomedical abstracts
headline_estimate: At least 13.5% of 2024 PubMed abstracts processed with LLMs (lower bound; up to 40% in some subcorpora)
verbatim_quote: This excess word analysis suggests that at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs.
notes: Journal version (Science Advances 2025, doi 10.1126/sciadv.adt3813). Duplicate of preprint arxiv:2406.07016 (posted June 2024, verified), same numbers; kept the journal version. Authors call 13.5% a lower bound that "differed across disciplines, countries, and journals, reaching 40% for some subcorpora".

title: Linguistic shifts in dental scientific writing in the large language model era.
corpus: 2,770 abstracts from six major dental journals
headline_estimate: High-suspicion abstracts (AI-marker score of 20 or more) rose from 18.0% to 25.8%; AI marker words per abstract rose from 0.69 to 0.97
verbatim_quote: The mean number of AI marker words per abstract rose from 0.69 to 0.97 (+41.1%), while high-suspicion abstracts (score ≥ 20) increased from 18.0% to 25.8% (+43%).
notes: Composite vocabulary score, not a share of LLM-written abstracts; 18.0% of abstracts were already "high-suspicion" in 2021 (pre-ChatGPT) on this score.

title: Have LLM-associated terms increased in article full texts in all fields?
corpus: 1.25 million MDPI articles (full text); 80 LLM-associated terms; 73 journals with 500+ articles in 2021 examined separately
headline_estimate: Term family "underscore" increased up to 29-fold; word-frequency change, not a share of papers
verbatim_quote: The term family "underscore" had the biggest increase: up to 29-fold.
notes: Reports term prevalence only; authors note some terms declined from 2024 to 2025 and uptake differs by journal (lower in the life sciences, higher in social sciences, electronic engineering and environmental science).

title: Quantifying large language model usage in scientific papers.
corpus: 1,121,912 preprints and published papers on arXiv, bioRxiv and Nature portfolio journals
headline_estimate: LLM-modified content up to 22% of computer science papers; up to 9% in mathematics and Nature portfolio
verbatim_quote: Our findings suggest a steady increase in LLM usage, with the largest and fastest growth estimated for computer science papers (up to 22%).
notes: Nature Human Behaviour 2025 (doi 10.1038/s41562-025-02273-8). Duplicate of preprint arxiv:2404.01268 (April 2024, verified), whose abstract reports 950,965 papers to February 2024 and up to 17.5% (computer science) and 6.3% (mathematics, Nature portfolio); kept the journal version with the later numbers. Same abstract: mathematics and Nature portfolio "up to 9%".

title: Em-ergence of the em-dash: a population-level rise in em-dash frequency in medRxiv preprints at the dawn of the large-language-model era
corpus: 69,632 first-version medRxiv preprints with an extractable Discussion section (full-text XML)
headline_estimate: Em-dash in Discussion sections rose from 4.23% of preprints before ChatGPT to 11.58% after (20.3% in 2025)
verbatim_quote: Em-dash prevalence in Discussion sections rose from 4.23% before ChatGPT to 11.58% afterward, an absolute increase of 7.35 percentage points (95% CI 6.94-7.77; odds ratio 2.96, 95% CI 2.77-3.17).
notes: Single punctuation marker, not a share of LLM text. Authors: "The em-dash is a population-level indicator, not a per-paper detector of LLM use, and the design cannot establish causality." Pre-registered (OSF HFT8C).

title: The evolution of ChatGPT-generated text in scientific medical publications.
corpus: 2,193,871 PubMed manuscripts; "delve" in title or abstract of 1,996
headline_estimate: At least 0.09% of all publications ChatGPT-generated, from the single word "delve"
verbatim_quote: The term "delve" was found in the title and abstract of 1996 scientific manuscripts, suggesting that at least 0.09% of all publications were ChatGPT-generated.
notes: Single-keyword floor on title and abstract only (Saudi Journal of Anaesthesia). Authors describe uncertain author auditing and editing.

title: Most biomedical publications show signs of LLM-assisted writing
corpus: Full texts of open-access biomedical papers from PubMed Central
headline_estimate: 89% of papers show excess LLM-associated vocabulary by end of 2025; 68% of Discussion paragraphs vs 32% of Methods paragraphs
verbatim_quote: We apply our method to the full texts of open-access biomedical papers from Pubmed Central, and show that by the end of 2025, 89% of papers show excess of LLM-associated vocabulary.
notes: Share of papers showing vocabulary excess, not share of text. Same abstract: "LLMs are twice as likely to be used when writing a paragraph in the Discussion section (68%) compared to a paragraph in the Methods section (32%), but even inside the Methods section, the overall prevalence of LLM usage is over 50%."

title: Large Language Model-Based Writing in Published Sports Medicine Research: Uncovering a Growing Influence.
corpus: 3,596 articles in the 5 highest-impact sports medicine journals after ChatGPT; 518 pre-ChatGPT articles used for the threshold
headline_estimate: 3.28% of post-ChatGPT articles exceeded a ZeroGPT threshold (rising from 2.38% in January 2023 to 6.25% in December 2024)
verbatim_quote: Among the 3596 articles published after the release of ChatGPT and included in this study, 3.28% exceeded the established threshold.
notes: ZeroGPT on full text with tables, figures and references removed; threshold 28.69% from pre-ChatGPT articles. Journal range 0.93% to 7.17%.

title: Increasing Use of Large Language Models for Scholarly Writing in Radiology.
corpus: Abstracts from radiology, surgery and internal medicine journals (number of abstracts not stated in the abstract)
headline_estimate: Proportion of LLM-modified text rose from 0.5% to 3.0% (radiology), 1.1% to 4.2% (surgery), 0.8% to 1.6% (internal medicine)
verbatim_quote: When comparing abstracts published before and after the ChatGPT release, the proportion of LLM-modified text increased for radiology journal articles from 0.5% to 3.0%, for surgery journal articles from 1.1% to 4.2%, and for internal medicine journal articles from 0.8% to 1.6%, respectively.
notes: AJR 2026. The PubMed abstract available to me contains only this results paragraph, so the method is not stated there (family set to "other"; wording suggests a corpus-level estimator but I did not read the method). Corpus size not read.

title: Almost Nobody Is Using ChatGPT to Write Academic Science Papers (Yet).
corpus: 19,000 scientific introductions from ten MDPI journals
headline_estimate: ChatGPT used for writing or significant editing in about 1 to 3% of introductions
verbatim_quote: We estimate that ChatGPT was used for writing or significant editing in about 1 to 3% of the introductions tested.
notes: Stylometric classifier ("stylistics" approach) applied to introductions only. Authors conclude "generative AI is not polluting mainstream journals to any appreciable extent".

title: Where there's a will there's a way: ChatGPT is used more for science in countries where it is prohibited
corpus: Preprints from arXiv, bioRxiv and medRxiv (corpus size not stated in abstract)
headline_estimate: ChatGPT used in about 12.6% of preprints by August 2023; 7.7% higher usage in restricted countries
verbatim_quote: Applying the classifier to preprints from Arxiv, BioRxiv, and MedRxiv showed ChatGPT was used in about 12.6% of preprints by August 2023, with 7.7% higher usage in restricted countries.
notes: Classifier trained on pre- and post-ChatGPT "polished" abstracts using distinctive word usage; authors report it outperformed GPTZero and ZeroGPT on validation sets.

title: Rise of AI-generated open-access review articles after ChatGPT: A case example in inflammatory bowel disease.
corpus: 180 open-access inflammatory bowel disease review articles from PubMed (60 per period)
headline_estimate: No articles AI-written before ChatGPT; 1.7% in the first year after, 6.7% in the year after that
verbatim_quote: Using an AI text detector, no articles were identified as AI-written in period 1, versus 1.7% and 6.7% in periods 2 and 3, respectively.
notes: Very small sample (60 per period); detector not named in the abstract. None of the flagged articles disclosed AI use.

title: ChatGPT "contamination": estimating the prevalence of LLMs in the scholarly literature
corpus: Scholarly literature (database not stated in the abstract); keywords disproportionately present in LLM text
headline_estimate: At least 60,000 papers, slightly over 1% of all articles, LLM-assisted in 2023
verbatim_quote: It is estimated that at least 60,000 papers (slightly over 1% of all articles) were LLM-assisted, though this number could be extended and refined by analysis of other characteristics of the papers or by identification of further indicative keywords.
notes: Keyword-based lower bound.

title: The Impact of AI on Scientific Literature: A Surge in AI-Associated Words in Academic and Biomedical Writing
corpus: PubMed and Scopus records for "delve", "realm" and "underscore"
headline_estimate: Co-use of "delve", "realm" and "underscore" up to 85-fold higher in 2023-2024 than in 2022 and earlier
verbatim_quote: The co-usage of these words increased by up to 85-fold in 2023 and 2024 compared to 2022 and prior years.
notes: medRxiv preprint. Fold-change in word co-occurrence, not a share of papers. Percentages in the abstract (e.g. "delve" in 44.0% of PubMed articles) are shares of all articles that ever used the word since 1849 and fall in 2023-2024, not shares of 2023-2024 papers.

title: Estimating the prevalence of LLM-assisted text in scholarly writing
corpus: Full text of published papers across all research fields indexed in Dimensions
headline_estimate: LLM tools likely involved in more than 10% of all published papers in 2024
verbatim_quote: It uses this to demonstrate that LLM tools are likely to have been involved in the production of more than 10% of all published papers in 2024, based on disproportionate use of specific indicative words, and draws together earlier studies to confirm that this is a plausible overall estimate.
notes: Full-text passage: the 12% Dimensions estimate "uses a more conservative methodology that requires at least two marker words"; summarising earlier work, 2024 all-field estimates of 7% and 9% (Nature-portfolio), 12% (Dimensions) and up to 16% (PubMed).

title: Recent Trend in Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Biomedical Publishing: A Quantitative Bibliometric Analysis.
corpus: 390 MEDLINE-indexed randomized-controlled-trial abstracts (30 per quarter)
headline_estimate: Abstracts with 90% or higher probability of AI-generated text rose from 21.7% to 36.7%
verbatim_quote: Among the 390 MEDLINE-indexed abstracts included in the analysis, the prevalence with a high probability (≥ 90%) of AI-generated text increased during the study period from 21.7% to 36.7% (p=0.01) based on a chi-square test for trend.
notes: Originality.AI. Authors note the increase was seen "even before the widespread adoption of ChatGPT"; the 21.7% starting level is a detector output, not a verified share. Reported detector: 100% sensitivity, 95% specificity.

title: Is ChatGPT Transforming Academics' Writing Style?
corpus: One million arXiv papers (abstracts)
headline_estimate: Fraction of LLM-style abstracts about 35% in computer science
verbatim_quote: We find that large language models (LLMs), represented by ChatGPT, are having an increasing impact on arXiv abstracts, especially in the field of computer science, where the fraction of LLM-style abstracts is estimated to be approximately 35%, if we take the responses of GPT-3.5 to one simple prompt, "revise the following sentences", as a baseline.
notes: Estimate depends on the baseline prompt ("revise the following sentences"); model calibrated on simulated ChatGPT-modified abstracts. No time point for the 35% is given in the abstract.

title: AI-generated text in otolaryngology publications: a comparative analysis before and after the release of ChatGPT.
corpus: 143 original articles from JAMA Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
headline_estimate: Mean percent AI-generated text rose from 34.36% to 46.53% in abstracts and from 32.43% to 45.08% in introductions
verbatim_quote: A significant increase was observed in the mean percentage of AI-generated text post-ChatGPT release, especially in the abstract (from 34.36 to 46.53%, p = 0.004), introduction (from 32.43 to 45.08%, p = 0.010), and discussion sections (from 15.73 to 25.03%, p = 0.015).
notes: ZeroGPT.com output averaged over articles; the pre-ChatGPT baseline is already 34.36% for abstracts, so the score is not a share of LLM-written text.

title: LLM Signals in Funded Grants: Evidence from International Funding Agencies
corpus: 221,425 funded grant abstracts from NSF (n = 96,020), NIH (n = 80,496) and UKRI (n = 44,909)
headline_estimate: Excess marker-word rate in post-ChatGPT grant abstracts of 4.0-8.4% (NSF), 1.4-3.7% (NIH), 2.8-6.8% (UKRI) above the pre-ChatGPT baseline
verbatim_quote: Taking the pre-ChatGPT 95th and 99th percentile marker rates within each agency as the baseline for naturally high marker density yields an excess in the post-period ranging from 4.0% to 8.4% at NSF, 1.4% to 3.7% at NIH, and 2.8% to 6.8% at UKRI.
notes: Quote from full-text passage (the arXiv abstract is cut before the results). Same text: mean marker rate rose from 274.7 to 417.1 per 100,000 tokens at NSF (51.9%), 266.6 to 339.3 at NIH (27.3%), 224.1 to 344.3 at UKRI (53.6%). Grant abstracts, not journal papers. Brief report.

title: The growing presence of AI-generated content in ophthalmology: a retrospective bibliographic analysis.
corpus: 1,036 manuscripts from 30 ophthalmology journals (519 before, 517 after December 2022)
headline_estimate: Mean AI probability score rose from 4.95% in 2022 to 11.2% by mid-2024
verbatim_quote: The mean AIPS rose from 4.95% in 2022 to 11.2% by mid-2024, with projections estimating 17.51% by mid-2026.
notes: Originality Standard 2.0.0 mean probability score, not a share of papers. "None of the included manuscripts disclosed AI usage, including 44 manuscripts with AIPS exceeding 25%."

title: What is the rate of text generated by artificial intelligence over a year of publication in Orthopedics & Traumatology: Surgery & Research? Analysis of 425 articles before versus after the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022.
corpus: 425 articles from Orthopaedics & Traumatology: Surgery & Research (221 before, 204 after November 2022)
headline_estimate: 10.1% of abstracts rated AI or considerable AI generation; mean AI generation in body plus abstract 10.30% before vs 15.64% after
verbatim_quote: AI-generated text was detected mainly in Abstracts, with a 10.1% rate of AI or considerable AI generation, compared to only 1.9% for the body of the article and 5.6% for the total body+abstract.
notes: ZeroGPT. Authors: use of translation software (Google Translate, DeepL) was associated with higher AI scores than a human translator, so scores are confounded.

title: Detectable AI-Generated Text in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery : A Comparison of 2014 and 2024 Publications.
corpus: 1,490 Journal of Craniofacial Surgery manuscripts (659 in 2014; 831 in 2024)
headline_estimate: Mean detectable AI content 8.6% in 2014 vs 10.7% in 2024
verbatim_quote: Mean detectable AI content increased from 8.6% (SD 9.8) in 2014 to 10.7% (SD 10.4) in 2024
notes: ZeroGPT. Authors: increase "likely reflecting detection software behavior and evolving writing structure rather than widespread use of generative AI"; 8.6% is the pre-LLM baseline.

title: An LLM-Associated Register Shift in Korean Journal Abstracts: A Morphology-Aware Excess-Vocabulary Study, 2018-2026
corpus: 398,296 Korean-language abstracts (KCI), with 47,165 Vietnamese abstracts for comparison
headline_estimate: Lower bound on LLM-processed Korean abstracts 3.5%, 10.5% and 16.1% for 2024-2026 (single-word); 7.8%, 20.6%, 33.0% (split-half set)
verbatim_quote: Under stated assumptions the single-word conditional lower bound on LLM-processed abstracts is 3.5%, 10.5% and 16.1% for 2024-2026 and a split-half set bound 7.8%, 20.6% and 33.0%.
notes: Korean-language corpus. Same abstract: Holzwarth et al.'s estimator under the same discipline gives 41.9% and 72.1% for 2025-2026; "implied prevalences are scenario-dependent"; placebo floors 0.1-2.2 points.

title: The Silent Author in Urology: Quantifying Large Language Model Influence at the Corpus Level
corpus: 64,444 unique abstracts from 38 urology journals (PubMed)
headline_estimate: Proportion of AI-like text 1.8% in 2020 and 5.3% in 2024
verbatim_quote: The proportion of AI-like text was negligible from 2010 to 2019, rising to 1.8% in 2020 and 5.3% in 2024.
notes: medRxiv preprint ("The Silent Author in Urology"). Mixture model against a 10,000-abstract GPT-3.5-turbo reference corpus. Authors report "Our validation calibration set showed an area under the curve of 0.5326" and a 1.8% estimate for 2020, before ChatGPT, so the estimate has a non-trivial baseline.

title: More than half of recent astronomy papers are written with language-model assistance
corpus: Full text of 207,111 astro-ph papers; 392 papers that disclose model use calibrate the assisted rate
headline_estimate: About 54% of 2025 astro-ph papers carry a language-model trace (at or above 36% under varied assumptions); 0.81% disclose it
verbatim_quote: For 2025 that gives 54⁺⁸₋₈ (stat, 95%) ⁺²⁶₋₀ (sys, background)% of papers, the second error being the spread across the three.
notes: Hierarchical Bayesian mixture model on marker-word counts. Authors: the answer "depends on how often these words would appear today if nobody used a model, a rate that must be modeled rather than observed"; marker excess "more than halves between 2023 and 2026" as authors adapt. Only 0.81% of 2025 papers disclose use.

title: Accelerated use of artificial intelligence-associated vocabulary in Japanese surgical journals after 2023.
corpus: Articles in Surgery Today and Surgical Case Reports
headline_estimate: Rare AI-related word density rose after 2023 (slope change beta = 1.05 per year); no share estimated
verbatim_quote: Rare-word density showed a marked post-2023 increase, with a significant change in slope (β = 1.05 per year, 95% CI: 1.01-1.10, p < 0.001).
notes: Interrupted time series on lexical marker density versus the pre-2023 trend; no share of LLM-written text is reported.

title: Rise of the Machines: The Prevalence and Disclosure of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Text in High-Impact Orthopaedic Journals.
corpus: 577 abstracts from five high-impact orthopaedic journals
headline_estimate: AI-generated text detected in 4.8% of abstracts (0% to 12% by journal)
verbatim_quote: AI-generated text was detected in 4.8% of abstracts, ranging from 0% to 12% by journal.
notes: Detector not named in the abstract; sensitivity 91.7% and specificity 100% on 60 pre-AI abstracts. Only 3.6% of the 28 flagged abstracts disclosed AI use.

title: Examining the frequency of artificial intelligence generated content in anesthesiology and intensive care journal publications: A cross sectional study.
corpus: 1,268 articles from 86 anesthesiology and intensive care journals (English abstracts)
headline_estimate: Mean AI usage 25.1% (ZeroGPT) and 10.5% (Copyleaks); 83.2% of articles labelled "AI-assisted"
verbatim_quote: ZeroGPT and Copyleaks found average AI usage at 25.1% ± 27.5 and 10.5% ± 15.9, respectively.
notes: Detector output on abstracts only; the two detectors differ by more than 2x and no validation against known human text is reported in the abstract. Authors label 83.2% of articles "AI-assisted" and 16.8% "human-written".

title: Prevalence of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Text in Neurosurgical Publications: Implications for Academic Integrity and Ethical Authorship.
corpus: 100 randomly selected manuscripts from high-impact neurosurgery journals
headline_estimate: About 20% of manuscripts contained sections flagged as AI-generated
verbatim_quote: Approximately one in five (20%) manuscripts contained sections flagged as AI-generated.
notes: Text flagged only if a RoBERTa-based classifier was positive and perplexity was below 100. Authors present the study as exposing "the fundamental limitations of current detection approaches".

title: Quantifying the Scope of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Writing in Orthopaedic Medical Literature: An Analysis of Prevalence and Validation of AI-Detection Software.
corpus: 240 randomly selected articles from six orthopaedic journals received after 1 January 2023, with 120 pre-ChatGPT negative controls and 36 altered positive controls
headline_estimate: Most accurate of three detectors showed +1.8% in percentage of text detected as AI after ChatGPT
verbatim_quote: The most accurate detector showed a modest increase in the percentage AI detected for the articles received post release of ChatGPT (+1.8%, P = 0.01).
notes: Authors: two of the three detectors "showed poor sensitivity and specificity". Reports a difference in detected percentage, not a level.

title: Analysis of Potential Generative AI Use in Abstracts of KAKENHI-Funded Projects
corpus: Abstracts of KAKENHI Scientific Research (C) funded projects (number not read)
headline_estimate: About 20% of FY2026 abstracts classified as AI-generated
verbatim_quote: The number of abstracts classified as AI-generated began to increase in FY2025, and approximately 20% of the abstracts were classified as AI-generated in FY2026.
notes: Japanese grant abstracts, not journal papers. Classifier (BERT) trained on abstracts regenerated by LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, Qwen3, Swallow). Full-text passage: with an alternative estimator "even in fiscal year 2022 ... 13.7% of the abstracts were classified as AI-generated", and "neither the absolute value ... nor the proportion exceeding the threshold of 0.5 should be interpreted directly as the rate of generative AI use".

title: Utilization of artificial intelligence-based writing assistance in contemporary spine literature.
corpus: 2,790 articles from six spine journals
headline_estimate: 25.7% of 2023-2024 spine articles had significant AI involvement
verbatim_quote: Among these spine journal articles, 25.7% were considered to have significant AI involvement.
notes: ZeroGPT; threshold 48.8% set at mean plus 2 SD of 2005 articles. Per the abstract, peak utilization was 32.0% at the start of 2023, with a plateau at 20.7% by the second quarter of 2024.

title: The Growing Role of Large Language Models in Arthroplasty Manuscripts: High-Productivity Authors Lead the Way.
corpus: 3,352 original research articles from six arthroplasty journals
headline_estimate: AI-flagged articles rose from under 4.2% (2018-2021) to 20.4% in 2025
verbatim_quote: The proportion of AI-flagged articles rose from less than 4.2% (2018 to 2021) to 20.4% in 2025, which was a notable nonlinear increase compared to 2024.
notes: Detection algorithm not named in the abstract; journal-specific threshold = pre-AI mean + 2 SD.

title: Rising Prevalence of Detected AI-Generated Text in Medical Literature: Longitudinal Analysis in Open Access Articles
corpus: 7,251 JAMA Network Open articles (Original Investigations, Research Letters, Invited Commentaries)
headline_estimate: 2.7% of articles classified as significantly AI-generated; monthly share 0.0% (Jan 2022) to 11.3% (Mar 2025)
verbatim_quote: Overall, 195 articles (2.7%) were classified as containing significant AI-generated text.
notes: Originality.AI. Authors: limitations of current detection tools necessitate cautious interpretation. Only 15 articles (0.2%) disclosed LLM use. Monthly proportion rose "from 0.0% in January 2022 to 11.3% in March 2025".

title: LLM-Generated or Human-Written? Comparing Review and Non-Review Papers on ArXiv
corpus: arXiv computer science papers, review vs non-review (number of papers not read)
headline_estimate: Estimated LLM use in CS papers 21.4% in review papers vs 14.0% in non-review papers
verbatim_quote: Over the past three years, we estimate the use of LLMs in CS papers to be 21.4% in review papers compared to 14.0% in non-review papers.
notes: Quote from full-text passage. Uses two methods (an "Alpha" distributional estimator and Pangram, a detector), so family set to "other". In 2025, 43.3% (review) vs 23.3% (non-review) using Pangram.

title: Large Language Model Authorship in Ophthalmic Publications.
corpus: Abstracts of 27,142 research articles from 22 ophthalmology journals (word-frequency screen); 50 full articles per journal scored with GPTZero
headline_estimate: By 2025, 25.7% of sampled research articles and 21.6% of commentaries had AI-likelihood scores more than 2 SD above baseline
verbatim_quote: By 2025, 25.7% of sampled research articles and 21.6% of commentary articles contained AI-likelihood scores of more than 2 standard deviations above the baseline.
notes: Combines excess vocabulary and GPTZero; the abstract also reports "at least a 2-fold usage increase observed in 20% of ophthalmology abstracts" for stylistic words. "Use of AI was not disclosed among any of the publications with outlier scores."

title: Evaluating the Prevalence of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Writing in Plastic Surgery Literature.
corpus: 1,627 manuscripts from 10 plastic surgery journals (300 pre-ChatGPT manuscripts from 2010-2011 set the threshold)
headline_estimate: 21.5% of 2024-2025 articles exceeded the threshold for substantial AI involvement (17% in 2024, 29% in 2025)
verbatim_quote: Overall, 21.5% of 2024-2025 articles exceeded the threshold for substantial AI involvement.
notes: ZeroGPT with a 22.5% threshold. Journal range 0-41%.

title: Evaluation of the impact of large language learning models on publications in the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery.
corpus: 232 Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery publications (114 from Jan-Apr 2022, 118 from Jan-Apr 2024)
headline_estimate: Abstracts with suspected AI percentage above 10%: 74.6% (2022) vs 86.4% (2024)
verbatim_quote: Abstracts with a suspected AI percentage > 10% constituted 74.6% of the publications in 2022 and 86.4% in 2024; P = .003.
notes: ZeroGPT and a ChatGPT detector. Full-body text showed no significant change (4.7% in 2022 vs 5.3% in 2024, P = .19); abstracts 21.1% vs 30.1%. A 74.6% pre-ChatGPT rate shows the >10% threshold mostly flags human text.

title: Estimating the use of ChatGPT in dental research publications.
corpus: 299,695 dental research abstracts indexed in PubMed
headline_estimate: Abstracts with ChatGPT "signaling words": 47.1 per 10,000 before release vs 224.2 per 10,000 after
verbatim_quote: Before ChatGPT's release, the frequency of abstracts with signaling words was 47.1 per 10,000 papers. After the release, this increased to 224.2 per 10,000 papers, an increase of 177.2 per 10,000 papers (p = 0.014, 95 % CI 53.5-300.7).
notes: Keyword analysis of titles and abstracts; frequency of abstracts containing any signalling word, not a share of LLM-written abstracts. "delve" showed the largest increase (ratio 17.0).

title: Towards the relationship between AIGC in manuscript writing and author profiles: evidence from preprints in LLMs
corpus: 4,889 arXiv preprints about LLMs first submitted in 2023 (abstracts of 100+ words)
headline_estimate: 7.3% (GPTKit) and 3.7% (Smodin) of abstracts had AI-generated probability above 0.9
verbatim_quote: While the AI-generated probability for most abstracts is very low and the number of papers decreases as the probability increases, a small proportion of papers (7.3% for GPTKIT and 3.7% for Smodin) exhibit an AI-generated probability greater than 0.9.
notes: Quote from full-text passage. Detectors disagree: "Sapling appears to focus more on the recall rate of AI-generated text, with 68.5% of abstracts having a GPT probability above 0.9"; 8.4% of papers contain words frequently used by AIGC tools.
